name: Practice With AI, Checks Without It
title: Practice With AI, Checks Without It
answer: Practice scores can climb while real learning stays flat, so a teacher cannot judge whether AI is helping from practice results alone. The fix is a regular rhythm of checks done without the tool, so the teacher can compare practice and unaided work for each student. This matters because students may lean on the tool without noticing, and they may not believe it has hurt them even when it has.

sections.body: This idea is about the gap between how well students perform during practice with AI and how much they actually learn. Practice scores can rise while real learning stays flat, a pattern seen in a high school math trial and again in a university programming course where students using AI scored higher on exercises but learned no more than students without it. In that study the students also preferred the tool that helped them least. Because of this, a teacher cannot rely on practice scores alone to know whether AI is helping. The solution is a regular rhythm of checks done without the tool, so practice results and unaided results can be compared.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a class might practice with an adaptive program or tutor on most days, then take a short quiz on paper each week. The teacher compares the two results for each student. When practice scores are high and quiz scores are low, the student may be leaning on the tool, and a conversation is in order. This rhythm also gives students honest information about what they can do on their own, which protects them from their own blind spots. Figure 7.4 shows a simple weekly pattern, and the text gives no separate grade band variations.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with evidence from two settings. In the high school math trial, students did not believe copying answers had hurt them, even though it had (Bastani et al., 2025). In a university programming course, students using AI scored higher on exercises but learned no more than students without it, and they preferred the tool that helped them least (Bassner et al., 2026). The text also refers to Figure 7.4, which shows a simple weekly pattern of practice with AI and checks without it.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are that practice scores alone can mislead, and that students may not recognise when the tool is doing the work for them. The decision to hold a conversation when practice scores are high and quiz scores are low stays with the teacher. The weekly check without AI is what gives students honest information about their own ability, so the judgement about what a student can do unaided remains a human one. Nothing here is legal advice, and this describes practice rather than a rule.
